---
title: "P5 exercises — Stress, defence and biotechnology"
---

The questions follow the [tutorial](index.qmd) and [slides](lec.qmd). Answer
each question before opening its answer.

## Abiotic stress

### 1.1

For each stress, name the main physiological problem it causes.

| Stress | Main problem |
| --- | --- |
| Drought | |
| Salinity | |
| Heat | |
| Freezing | |

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

| Stress | Main problem |
| --- | --- |
| Drought | Low soil water potential; reduced water uptake and loss of turgor |
| Salinity | Osmotic effect (low soil water potential) plus ion toxicity, mainly from Na⁺ and Cl⁻ |
| Heat | Protein denaturation and increased membrane fluidity |
| Freezing | Ice formation in extracellular spaces dehydrates cells; ice crystals can damage membranes |
:::

### 1.2

Which hormone accumulates in leaves during drought, and what is its main
immediate effect?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Abscisic acid (ABA). It causes stomatal closure, which reduces transpiration.
:::

### 1.3

What is the cost to the plant of the response in 1.2?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Closed stomata also reduce CO₂ uptake, so photosynthesis falls. Less
transpiration also means less evaporative cooling, so leaf temperature rises.
:::

### 1.4

Name two kinds of compatible solutes, and explain how accumulating them helps
a plant under drought or salinity.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Examples are proline, glycine betaine and sugars or sugar alcohols such as
sucrose and mannitol. They lower the cell's solute potential, so the cell can
keep taking up water from a soil with low water potential. They do so without
inhibiting enzymes.
:::

### 1.5

Name two classes of proteins induced by heat or drought stress that help
protect cells.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Heat shock proteins (chaperones that refold or stabilise proteins) and
dehydrins/LEA (late embryogenesis abundant) proteins. Antioxidant enzymes such
as superoxide dismutase and catalase are also accepted.
:::

### 1.6

Reactive oxygen species (ROS) can damage cells. Name one other role they play
in plants.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Signalling. For example, ROS act in stress signalling, stomatal closure and
defence against pathogens.
:::

### 1.7

Classify each as acclimation or evolutionary adaptation.

a. Plants of a species become more freezing-tolerant after two weeks at 4 °C.
b. A population on saline coastal soil has heritably higher salt tolerance
   than inland populations grown under the same conditions.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. Acclimation (cold acclimation). b. Evolutionary adaptation.
:::

## Biotic stress and defence

### 2.1

Name two constitutive (pre-existing) defences and two induced defences of plants.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Constitutive: the cuticle, cell walls, thorns or trichomes, and stored
specialised metabolites. Induced: callose deposition, phytoalexin production,
proteinase inhibitors, and the hypersensitive response.
:::

### 2.2

Match each attacker to the main defence hormone pathway: salicylic acid (SA)
or jasmonic acid (JA).

a. A biotrophic pathogen that feeds on living tissue
b. A chewing caterpillar
c. A necrotrophic fungus that kills tissue before feeding on it

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. SA. b. JA. c. JA, together with ethylene. The SA and JA pathways often
act antagonistically.
:::

### 2.3

What is the hypersensitive response, and why is it effective against biotrophic
pathogens?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

It is rapid, localised death of the plant cells at the infection site. A
biotrophic pathogen needs living host cells, so killing the infected cells
deprives it of nutrients and limits its spread.
:::

### 2.4

What is systemic acquired resistance (SAR), and which hormone is required for it?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

SAR is long-lasting, broad-spectrum resistance in uninfected parts of the plant
after a local infection. It requires salicylic acid.
:::

### 2.5

Name the three major classes of plant specialised (secondary) metabolites,
and give one example of each.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

- Terpenoids, e.g. pyrethrins, essential oils such as menthol, or carotenoids.
- Phenolics, e.g. flavonoids, tannins or lignin.
- Nitrogen-containing compounds, e.g. alkaloids such as nicotine, caffeine
  or morphine, and cyanogenic glycosides.
:::

### 2.6

Why are many defence compounds stored as inactive precursors, such as
glucosinolates or cyanogenic glycosides?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

The active compound is toxic to the plant itself. The precursor is stored
separately from the activating enzyme, and they meet only when tissue is
damaged by a herbivore. The toxin is therefore released only at the site of
attack.
:::

### 2.7

True or false? Correct any false statements.

a. Defence compounds use carbon and nitrogen that could otherwise be used for growth.
b. A plant with constitutively activated jasmonate signalling grows larger
   than a wild-type plant.
c. Natural plant compounds are harmless to humans.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. True. This is the basis of the growth–defence trade-off.
b. False. Constitutive defence activation usually reduces growth.
c. False. Many, such as nicotine, ricin or cyanogenic glycosides, are toxic.
:::

## Model systems

### 3.1

Give three properties that make *Arabidopsis thaliana* a useful model plant.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Any three of: a short life cycle (about 6–8 weeks); small size; a small,
fully sequenced genome; self-pollination; many seeds; easy transformation
with *Agrobacterium* (floral dip); large collections of mutants.
:::

## Transformation and tissue culture

### 4.1

Put the steps of *Agrobacterium*-mediated transformation in order.

a. Regenerate whole plants from the transformed cells
b. Insert the gene of interest into the T-DNA of a binary vector
c. Select transformed cells on medium containing an antibiotic or herbicide
d. Co-cultivate plant explants with *Agrobacterium*
e. Confirm the insertion and expression of the transgene

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

b → d → c → a → e.
:::

### 4.2

What is a selectable marker gene? Give an example.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

It is a gene, transferred together with the gene of interest, that allows only
transformed cells to survive on a selective medium. Examples are *nptII*
(kanamycin resistance), *hpt* (hygromycin resistance) and *bar* (resistance
to the herbicide glufosinate).
:::

### 4.3

What is the difference between stable transformation and transient expression?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

In stable transformation, the transgene is integrated into the plant genome
and inherited by the offspring. In transient expression, the introduced DNA
is expressed for a few days without integration and is not inherited.
:::

### 4.4

Name a method for delivering DNA into plant cells that does not use
*Agrobacterium*.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Particle bombardment (biolistics). Protoplast transformation, using
polyethylene glycol or electroporation, is also accepted.
:::

### 4.5

What property of plant cells makes it possible to regenerate a whole plant
from a single transformed cell?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Totipotency: many differentiated plant cells can dedifferentiate and
regenerate all the organs of a whole plant.
:::

### 4.6

In tissue culture, what does an explant form at each auxin-to-cytokinin ratio?

a. High auxin : cytokinin
b. Intermediate (roughly balanced)
c. Low auxin : cytokinin (high cytokinin)

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. Roots. b. Undifferentiated callus. c. Shoots. The exact concentrations
depend on species and tissue.
:::

### 4.7

Why must several independent transgenic lines be analysed, rather than one?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

The T-DNA inserts at a random position in the genome. It can disrupt or
activate a native gene, and tissue culture can itself cause mutations
(somaclonal variation). A phenotype seen consistently in independent lines
is more likely to be caused by the transgene.
:::

## Promoters and reporters

### 5.1

Match each promoter type to its expression pattern.

| Promoter | Pattern |
| --- | --- |
| a. Constitutive (e.g. CaMV 35S) | 1. Expressed only after exposure to a signal |
| b. Tissue-specific | 2. Expressed in nearly all tissues at all times |
| c. Inducible | 3. Expressed only in particular cell types, e.g. guard cells |

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a–2, b–3, c–1.
:::

### 5.2

Name two reporter genes used in plants, and how each one is detected.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

- GUS (β-glucuronidase): a blue product after staining with X-Gluc.
- GFP (green fluorescent protein): fluorescence under blue/UV light.
- Luciferase: light emission when luciferin is supplied.
:::

## Genetically modified crops

### 6.1

Match each GM trait to the gene or mechanism used.

| Trait | Gene or mechanism |
| --- | --- |
| a. Insect resistance | 1. Bacterial EPSP synthase insensitive to glyphosate |
| b. Herbicide tolerance | 2. Carotenoid biosynthesis genes in the endosperm |
| c. Golden Rice | 3. *Cry* toxin gene from *Bacillus thuringiensis* |

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a–3, b–1, c–2. Golden Rice makes β-carotene (provitamin A) in the grain.
:::

### 6.2

How does the Bt (Cry) protein kill insect larvae, and why is it harmless to
mammals?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

In the alkaline gut of susceptible larvae, the protoxin is activated by
proteases. It binds to specific receptors on the gut epithelium and forms
pores, so the gut cells lyse. Mammals have an acidic stomach and lack these
receptors.
:::

### 6.3

What is a refuge strategy in Bt crop cultivation, and what problem does it delay?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Non-Bt plants are grown next to the Bt crop. Susceptible insects survive on
the refuge and mate with any resistant insects, which keeps the resistance
alleles rare. This delays the evolution of Bt resistance in the pest.
:::

### 6.4

How does genome editing with CRISPR–Cas9 differ from classical transgenesis?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Classical transgenesis inserts foreign DNA into the genome. CRISPR–Cas9 makes
a targeted cut in an existing gene, which can create a small mutation in that
gene. The Cas9 construct can then be removed by crossing, so the final plant
may contain no foreign DNA.
:::

### 6.5

Classify each question as empirical (it can be answered by measurement) or
value-based.

a. Does pollen from a GM crop reach a wild relative 100 m away?
b. How much uncertainty about environmental effects is acceptable?
c. Does a Bt crop reduce insecticide use in a region?
d. Who should decide whether a GM crop is grown?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. Empirical. b. Value-based. c. Empirical. d. Value-based.
:::

## Explore: Stomata, ABA and drought {#explore-p5-stomata}

The demo shows a stoma closing as ABA rises in the guard cells, and how
conductance, water loss, CO₂ uptake, CO₂ gained per water lost and leaf
temperature (leaf minus air) change. Use the drought buttons or the ABA
slider; "Air dryness" sets the vapour pressure deficit (VPD) of the air. The
curves show water loss and CO₂ uptake as % of the fully open value.

```{=html}
<link rel="stylesheet" href="../../demos/dist/demo.css">
<div data-demo="p5-stomata" data-aba="0" data-vpd="2"></div>
<script src="../../demos/dist/p5-stomata.js"></script>
```

### E1.1

Keep air dryness at 2 kPa. Fill in the table from the readout for "Well
watered", "Mild drought" and "Severe drought".

| | Conductance (mol m⁻² s⁻¹) | Water loss (mmol m⁻² s⁻¹) | CO₂ uptake (µmol m⁻² s⁻¹) | Leaf − air (°C) |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Well watered (ABA 0) | | | | |
| Mild drought (ABA 1) | | | | |
| Severe drought (ABA 4) | | | | |

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

| | Conductance | Water loss | CO₂ uptake | Leaf − air |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Well watered (ABA 0) | 0.50 | 9.9 | 28.0 | −0.8 |
| Mild drought (ABA 1) | 0.25 | 4.9 | 22.6 | +4.2 |
| Severe drought (ABA 4) | 0.03 | 0.6 | 5.7 | +8.5 |

Less transpiration means less evaporative cooling, so the leaf warms: with
severe drought it is about 8 °C above air temperature.
:::

### E1.2

Compare well watered with mild drought.

a. By what percentage does water loss fall, and by what percentage does
   CO₂ uptake fall?
b. Does CO₂ gained per water lost increase or decrease? Give both values.
c. Why does CO₂ uptake fall less than water loss?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. Water loss falls by 50 % (9.9 → 4.9); CO₂ uptake falls by only about
   20 % (28.0 → 22.6).
b. It increases, from 2.8 to 4.6 µmol CO₂ per mmol H₂O.
c. Water loss is proportional to stomatal conductance, but CO₂ uptake is
   limited by two steps in series, the stomata and carboxylation in the
   chloroplast. Partly closing the stomata therefore costs less carbon than
   water.
:::

### E1.3

Set ABA to 0 and move air dryness from 2 to 4 kPa. Which of these change:
conductance, water loss, CO₂ uptake, leaf temperature? Give the new water
loss.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Water loss doubles to 19.7 mmol m⁻² s⁻¹ and the leaf cools (to −10.7 °C
relative to the air). Conductance (0.50) and CO₂ uptake (28.0) do not change:
in this model dry air drives transpiration through the same open stomata.
Real plants also close their stomata partly in dry air.
:::

## Explore: Auxin and cytokinin in tissue culture {#explore-p5-tissueculture}

An explant grows on a medium with auxin and cytokinin. Set the two
concentrations with the sliders (log scale, mg/L), drag the dot on the map,
or use the preset buttons; the dish shows the explant after four weeks and
the readout gives the outcome and the auxin : cytokinin ratio. "Infected by
wild Agrobacterium" adds the hormones that a crown-gall T-DNA makes inside
the plant cells. The model is a rule of thumb, not fitted to data.

```{=html}
<link rel="stylesheet" href="../../demos/dist/demo.css">
<div data-demo="p5-tissueculture" data-auxin="0.3" data-cytokinin="0.3"></div>
<script src="../../demos/dist/p5-tissueculture.js"></script>
```

### E2.1

Press each preset and record the outcome and the auxin : cytokinin ratio:
Rooting, Callus, Shoots, No hormones.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

| Preset | Auxin (mg/L) | Cytokinin (mg/L) | Ratio | Outcome |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Rooting | 2.0 | 0.020 | 100 | Roots |
| Callus | 1.0 | 1.0 | 1.0 | Callus |
| Shoots | 0.032 | 2.0 | 0.02 | Shoots |
| No hormones | 0.010 | 0.010 | 1.0 | Little growth |

High auxin : cytokinin gives roots, low gives shoots, and a balance gives
undifferentiated callus (Skoog and Miller). The No-hormones medium has the
same ratio as Callus, but too little of either hormone for growth: the
absolute level matters too.
:::

### E2.2

Set cytokinin to 0.10 mg/L and auxin to 0.10 mg/L, then raise auxin in steps.
At what auxin concentration does the outcome first change from Callus, and
to what? What is the ratio then?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

At 0.56 mg/L auxin it changes to "Roots from callus" (ratio 5.6); from
0.71 mg/L it is "Roots". Up to 0.50 mg/L (ratio 5.0) the explant forms only
callus. Swapping the two hormones gives the mirror result: shoots from
callus once cytokinin reaches 0.56 mg/L at 0.10 mg/L auxin.
:::

### E2.3

Press "No hormones" and tick "Infected by wild Agrobacterium". What does the
explant form? Then press "Rooting" with the box still ticked: what is the
outcome and the ratio now?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

With no hormones in the medium it forms a tumour (crown gall), with ratio
1.0. On the rooting medium it is still a tumour, and the ratio falls from
100 to 2.9. The wild T-DNA carries genes for auxin and cytokinin synthesis,
so the infected cells make their own hormones and proliferate whatever the
medium. Disarmed strains used for transformation lack these genes.
:::

## Explore: Refuges and Bt resistance {#explore-p5-refuge}

The demo follows the frequency of a resistance allele R in a pest over
generations. Bt maize kills 99 % of susceptible (SS) larvae; a refuge of
non-Bt maize lets all genotypes survive, and adults from both mate at
random. Set the refuge size, the dominance of R (h = 0: recessive, h = 1:
dominant) and the starting frequency of R. The readout gives the number of
generations until R reaches 50 % and the fitness of each genotype.

```{=html}
<link rel="stylesheet" href="../../demos/dist/demo.css">
<div data-demo="p5-refuge" data-refuge="0" data-h="0" data-p0="0.001"></div>
<script src="../../demos/dist/p5-refuge.js"></script>
```

### E3.1

Keep the starting frequency at 0.001 and h = 0. How many generations does it
take for R to reach 50 % with no refuge, a 5 % refuge, a 10 % refuge and a
20 % refuge?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

| Refuge | Generations to 50 % R |
| ---: | ---: |
| 0 % | 15 |
| 5 % | 70 |
| 10 % | 129 |
| 20 % | more than 150 |

Susceptible adults from the refuge mate with the rare resistant survivors,
so most R alleles end up in RS offspring, which are killed on Bt maize when R
is recessive.
:::

### E3.2

Press "20% refuge", then "20%, dominant R". Read off the generations to 50 %
and the fitness of RS for each. Which is the more important condition for the
refuge to work?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

| | RS fitness | Generations to 50 % R |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| 20 % refuge, h = 0 | 0.208 | more than 150 |
| 20 % refuge, h = 1 | 1.000 | 6 |

With dominant resistance, RS larvae survive on Bt maize as well as RR, and
the refuge no longer slows resistance (6 generations, faster even than no
refuge with a recessive allele). The refuge strategy therefore requires a
high-dose Bt crop that kills heterozygotes, which makes R effectively
recessive.
:::

### E3.3

Set a 20 % refuge, h = 0, and the starting frequency of R to 0.01 instead of
0.001. How many generations does R take to reach 50 %?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

31 generations (compared with more than 150 at 0.001). The refuge works best
when R is very rare, because almost all R alleles are then in heterozygotes.
Refuges must be in place from the first Bt planting, not added after
resistance has been detected.
:::

## R and bioinformatics {#r-exercises}

Run the code in R or RStudio. Only base R is used (no packages), and all data
are typed into the code.

### R1. Growth of watered and drought-stressed plants

The heights below are invented teaching data (the course file
`data/growth-stress.csv`): pots 1–6 were watered and pots 7–12 received
reduced water for 7 days. Run the code. What are the mean growth and the
standard deviation (to two decimals) in each group?

```r
initial <- c(30, 32, 28, 31, 29, 30, 31, 29, 30, 32, 28, 30)
final   <- c(48, 52, 50, 50, 50, 50, 41, 41, 44, 43, 41, 42)
growth  <- final - initial
growth
watered <- growth[1:6]
drought <- growth[7:12]
mean(watered)
mean(drought)
round(sd(watered), 2)
round(sd(drought), 2)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

```
 [1] 18 20 22 19 21 20 10 12 14 11 13 12
[1] 20
[1] 12
[1] 1.41
[1] 1.41
```

Watered: mean 20 mm, SD 1.41 mm. Reduced water: mean 12 mm, SD 1.41 mm.
R subtracts the two vectors element by element, pot by pot.
:::

### R2. Is the difference larger than chance? A t-test

Put the growth values from R1 in a data frame and compare the groups with a
t-test. Run the code. How many rows does the subset show, what are the t
value and the p-value, and is the difference significant at the 0.05 level:
(a) yes or (b) no?

```r
pots <- data.frame(
  treatment = rep(c("watered", "reduced-water"), each = 6),
  growth_mm = c(18, 20, 22, 19, 21, 20, 10, 12, 14, 11, 13, 12)
)
pots[pots$treatment == "reduced-water", ]
result <- t.test(growth_mm ~ treatment, data = pots)
result
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

```
       treatment growth_mm
7  reduced-water        10
8  reduced-water        12
9  reduced-water        14
10 reduced-water        11
11 reduced-water        13
12 reduced-water        12

	Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  growth_mm by treatment
t = -9.798, df = 10, p-value = 1.916e-06
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group reduced-water and group watered is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -9.819268 -6.180732
sample estimates:
mean in group reduced-water       mean in group watered 
                         12                          20 
```

Six rows. t = −9.798, p = 1.916 × 10⁻⁶. (a) yes, p is far below 0.05.
The t value is negative because R puts the groups in alphabetical order and
subtracts watered from reduced-water. The test says the growth difference is
unlikely to be chance; it does not say whether the plants would recover or
set fewer seeds.
:::

### R3. Resistance evolution on a Bt crop

The loop follows the frequency `p` of a resistance allele R in an insect
population feeding on a Bt crop. Fitness values are invented teaching
numbers: RR larvae survive (`w_RR = 1`) and 10 % of SS larvae survive
(`w_SS = 0.1`).

a. Run the code with `w_RS <- 1` (R dominant). What is the frequency of R
   after one generation (to four decimals), and after how many generations
   does it first exceed 0.5?
b. Change to `w_RS <- 0.1` (R recessive, as with a high-dose Bt crop). What
   does the last line print, and what does that mean?
c. Keep `w_RS <- 0.1` and change both `30`s to `200`. After how many
   generations does R first exceed 0.5?

```r
p <- 0.001
w_RR <- 1; w_RS <- 1; w_SS <- 0.1
p_values <- p
for (gen in 1:30) {
  q <- 1 - p
  w_bar <- p^2 * w_RR + 2 * p * q * w_RS + q^2 * w_SS
  p <- (p^2 * w_RR + p * q * w_RS) / w_bar
  p_values <- c(p_values, p)
}
round(p_values[2], 4)
which(p_values > 0.5)[1] - 1
plot(0:30, p_values, type = "l", xlab = "Generation", ylab = "Frequency of R")
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. 
   ```
   [1] 0.0098
   [1] 4
   ```
   R rises from 0.001 to 0.0098 in one generation and exceeds 0.5 after
   4 generations.
b. 
   ```
   [1] 0.001
   [1] NA
   ```
   `NA` means no generation in the first 30 had a frequency above 0.5; R is
   still about 0.001.
c. 
   ```
   [1] 0.001
   [1] 118
   ```
   118 generations. When RS larvae die like SS larvae, almost all rare R
   alleles (which sit in heterozygotes) are removed, so resistance spreads
   far more slowly. `p_values[1]` is generation 0, which is why the code
   subtracts 1.
:::

### R4. Finding a CRISPR guide next to a PAM

Cas9 cuts a DNA target that is directly followed by an NGG PAM (any base,
then GG). A guide RNA matches the 20 nucleotides just before the PAM. The
target below is a made-up sequence. Run the code. At which positions do
NGG sites start, what is the 20-nucleotide guide before the first PAM, and
what is its GC content (%)?

```r
target <- "ATGCTAGCTTGACCGTAGCATCGGATCCAGTTAACGG"
pam <- as.vector(gregexpr("(?=[ACGT]GG)", target, perl = TRUE)[[1]])
pam
guide <- substr(target, pam[1] - 20, pam[1] - 1)
guide
bases <- strsplit(guide, "")[[1]]
gc <- mean(bases == "G" | bases == "C") * 100
gc
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

```
[1] 22 35
[1] "TGCTAGCTTGACCGTAGCAT"
[1] 50
```

NGG sites start at positions 22 (CGG) and 35 (CGG). The guide is
TGCTAGCTTGACCGTAGCAT (positions 2–21), with 50 % GC (10 of 20 bases are G
or C). The pattern `(?=...)` lets R also report overlapping matches.
:::

### R5. Checking the edit: percent identity

After editing, the target region of a plant is sequenced and aligned with
the wild type. Both are made-up sequences; `-` marks a gap. Run the code.
How many aligned positions are identical, what is the percent identity (to
one decimal), and at which position is the difference? Is the edit
(a) a substitution, (b) a 1-base deletion or (c) a 1-base insertion, and does
it shift the reading frame?

```r
wild_type <- "ATGGCTTCAGGATCCAGTTAAGCT"
edited    <- "ATGGCTTCAGGAT-CAGTTAAGCT"
a <- strsplit(wild_type, "")[[1]]
b <- strsplit(edited, "")[[1]]
length(a)
sum(a == b)
round(sum(a == b) / length(a) * 100, 1)
which(a != b)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

```
[1] 24
[1] 23
[1] 95.8
[1] 14
```

23 of 24 positions are identical, 95.8 % identity, and the difference is at
position 14. (b) a 1-base deletion: the C in the wild type faces a gap in
the edited sequence. One base is not a multiple of three, so the reading
frame shifts after the deletion. High percent identity therefore does not
mean the protein is nearly unchanged.
:::
